prompt_text: I need a dental implant in Denver. Which specific dental practices should I call, and why?
q1_prompt_text: Who is the best dentist in Denver for a dental implant?
competitors_mentioned: ClearChoice Dental Implant Center – Denver area
American College of Prosthodontists Find a Prosthodontist
University of Colorado School of Dental Medicine
engine_stated_criteria: “What implant brand do you use, and will I receive the implant records?”
“How do you handle complications or an implant that does not integrate?”
answer_verbatim:
No one office is “best” for every implant case, but in Denver I’d start by calling these practices/clinics based on the kind of treatment you need:

| Practice to call | Best fit | Why call |
|---|---|---|
| **Colorado Surgical Arts** (Denver metro locations) | Single implant, extraction + implant, bone grafting, sedation, more surgical/complex cases | They are an oral and maxillofacial surgery group, so they are a strong first call if you need an extraction, graft, sinus lift, IV sedation, or have limited bone. Ask whether they coordinate the final crown with your regular dentist or provide a restorative partner. |
| **University of Colorado School of Dental Medicine, Anschutz Medical Campus** (Aurora) | Complex medical history, second opinion, lower-cost teaching-clinic route, difficult cases | The dental school has specialists and faculty oversight in periodontics, prosthodontics, and oral/maxillofacial surgery. It can be a particularly good option if you need a multidisciplinary plan—not just “place an implant”—or want another opinion on a complicated case. Treatment can take longer than a private office. |
| **Mile High Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery** (Denver metro) | Surgical implant placement, grafting, anesthesia/sedation | Another oral-surgery-focused option worth comparing with Colorado Surgical Arts. Especially sensible if you have impacted teeth, prior failed dental work, bone loss, anxiety about the procedure, or may need sedation. |
| **ClearChoice Dental Implant Center – Denver area** | Several missing teeth, failing dentition, implant-supported bridge, “All-on-4/All-on-X” full-arch work | This is the one I’d call if you are considering a full upper or lower arch rather than one missing tooth. Their model is built around full-mouth implant cases and coordinating surgery with the final fixed teeth. Get a detailed written quote and compare it with at least one independent prosthodontist/oral-surgery team. |
| **A prosthodontist-led practice in Denver** | Front-tooth implant, cosmetic-zone implant, multiple teeth, bite problems, final crown/bridge design matters most | For an implant that will show when you smile—or a bridge/full-mouth restoration—the final teeth should drive the surgical plan. Use the **American College of Prosthodontists “Find a Prosthodontist”** directory for a Denver provider, then ask whether they place implants themselves or work with a local surgeon. |

## My practical call order

### If you need **one tooth replaced**
1. **Your current general dentist** — ask who they use for implant planning and who will make the final crown.  
2. **Colorado Surgical Arts** or **Mile High Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery** — for the surgical opinion.  
3. A **Denver prosthodontist** if the tooth is in the smile zone, you have gum recession, or you care heavily about aesthetics.

For a single straightforward implant, a surgeon placing the implant plus a skilled restorative dentist making the crown is often an excellent arrangement.

### If you need **multiple teeth or full-mouth implants**
1. **ClearChoice Denver-area center** — obtain a full-arch consultation and written proposal.  
2. **University of Colorado School of Dental Medicine** — get an independent second opinion, especially if you have bone loss, diabetes, smoking history, sleep apnea, or previous implant failure.  
3. **Colorado Surgical Arts** plus a prosthodontist/restorative dentist — compare a specialist-team plan against the full-arch center’s plan.

## What to ask each office on the first call

Ask these questions before paying for a consultation:

1. **“Do you handle my type of case—single tooth / multiple teeth / full arch—and who actually places the implant?”**  
   Look for an oral surgeon, periodontist, or appropriately experienced implant dentist.

2. **“Who designs and delivers the final crown or bridge?”**  
   This matters as much as the surgery. You want the surgeon and restorative dentist to communicate before placement.

3. **“Will I need a 3-D CBCT scan, extraction, bone graft, sinus lift, temporary tooth, or sedation?”**  
   Ask whether each is included in the quote.

4. **“Can you give me an itemized written estimate from extraction through final crown?”**  
   A quoted “implant price” often excludes the abutment, crown, grafting, scan, temporary tooth, and follow-up visits.

5. **“What implant brand do you use, and will I receive the implant records?”**  
   Established systems with readily available parts are preferable, particularly if you move or need care years later.

6. **“How do you handle complications or an implant that does not integrate?”**  
   Ask about the office’s policy on replacement surgery and whether lab/restorative fees are separate.

7. **“Do you submit insurance, offer financing, and is the consultation/CBCT fee applied to treatment?”**  
   Dental insurance often contributes little or nothing toward the implant fixture itself, though it may help with the crown or extraction.

## A quick caution

Be cautious with any office that gives a firm implant price without examining you or reviewing a 3-D scan, pressures you into same-day treatment, or cannot clearly explain who will make the final tooth. For implants, the lowest initial quote is often not the lowest total cost.

If you tell me whether this is **one tooth, several teeth, or a full arch**, plus your neighborhood and whether budget/insurance or sedation is important, I can narrow this to the best 2–3 calls.
